package_info.why_malicious: The package is a typosquatting attack designed to impersonate the legitimate 'ionicons' package. It contains obfuscated JavaScript that, when included in a web application, intercepts user form submissions and exfiltrates sensitive data (such as credentials and personally identifiable information) to attacker-controlled domains. This behavior is entirely unrelated to the expected functionality of an icon/UI library and constitutes a severe data theft risk.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (in-browser execution when user interacts with forms)
execution_context.file_location: main JavaScript bundle included in the application via the malicious npm package

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code attaches 'submit' event listeners to all form elements in the DOM, collects the submitted form data, and sends it via HTTPS POST to a hardcoded attacker-controlled domain (ionicio.com), resulting in exfiltration of user-entered data.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code intercepts all form submissions and exfiltrates the complete form data to an external, attacker-controlled domain without user consent or notification. This is a classic data theft technique and is highly suspicious, especially in a package that should only provide UI icons.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate UI icon packages are expected to provide static assets or UI components and should not access, intercept, or transmit user form data. The presence of code that manipulates form submissions and sends data to unrelated domains is a clear violation of expected package behavior.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate applications may send form data to their own backend servers for processing, but never to unrelated or suspicious external domains, and never from a package whose purpose is unrelated to data handling.
key_indicators: Attaches event listeners to all form elements in the DOM
Collects and serializes form data on submission
Sends form data to a hardcoded, attacker-controlled domain (e.g., ionicio.com)
Obfuscated or minified code to conceal intent
No user notification or consent for data transmission
Behavior present in a package claiming to be a UI/icon library

attack_chain.action: Developer installs the malicious npm package (icon-package) due to typosquatting, mistaking it for the legitimate 'ionicons' package.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is included in the application's dependency tree.

attack_chain.action: Application is built and deployed with the malicious package; end-users load the application in their browsers.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious JavaScript is executed in the end-user's browser environment.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code attaches 'submit' event listeners to all forms and intercepts form submissions.
attack_chain.leads_to: Form data is captured at the point of user submission.

attack_chain.action: Captured form data is exfiltrated to attacker-controlled domains (e.g., ionicio.com) via HTTPS POST requests.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives sensitive user data (credentials, PII, etc.)

behavioral_signatures: JavaScript code in UI/icon packages that attaches event listeners to all forms and sends form data to external domains
Obfuscated or minified code containing network requests to suspicious or non-canonical domains
Unexpected network activity originating from packages whose primary function is to provide static assets or UI components
file_indicators: Presence of obfuscated JavaScript in packages claiming to be UI/icon libraries
References to external domains (e.g., ionicio.com, graph-googleapis.com) in package source code or bundled assets
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor npm packages, especially those purporting to be UI/icon libraries, for the presence of obfuscated JavaScript that makes network requests to domains not associated with the legitimate package. Flag any code that attaches event listeners to all forms and sends form data to external, non-canonical domains. Use network monitoring to detect exfiltration attempts to the listed IOC domains. Automated static analysis should look for suspicious domain references and event listener patterns in package code.
